claims.text: Rapid formation of a protective oxide layer in high-temperature HEAs is driven by differential diffusion of multiple oxide-forming elements.
Long-term retention of a protective oxide layer in high-temperature HEAs is driven by differential diffusion of multiple oxide-forming elements.
Slower-diffusing elements such as Cr or Al preferentially enrich at the oxide/alloy interface.
Interfacial enrichment of Cr or Al controls the formation kinetics and stability of the protective oxide scale.
The proposed starting material is a homogeneous as-cast or wrought HEA with uniformly distributed principal elements, including Cr and Al.
Systematically varying Cr and Al concentration is proposed as the intervention.
The comparison is to be conducted at 800–1200°C under a controlled oxidizing atmosphere.
Localized enrichment of slower-diffusing oxide-forming elements promotes development of a dense and adherent protective oxide scale.
Localized enrichment of slower-diffusing oxide-forming elements promotes persistence of the protective oxide scale.
Differential diffusion rates among HEA constituents produce selective elemental partitioning.
Cr or Al builds up at the surface and rapidly reacts with oxygen to form a stable protective oxide.
The proposed enrichment mechanism is less effective in simpler binary alloys because controlled diffusion and partitioning are less pronounced in them.
HEAs with higher concentrations of slower-diffusing oxide formers will develop a more uniform and adherent protective oxide layer than baseline simpler alloys.
HEAs with higher concentrations of slower-diffusing oxide formers will have lower oxidation rates than baseline simpler alloys with comparable oxide-former content.
The expected behavior applies from 800–1200°C at controlled oxygen partial pressures and may not apply at lower temperatures or in non-oxidizing atmospheres.
Prior oxidation studies support a role for differential diffusion and selective enrichment.
The quantitative relationships among elemental concentration, diffusion rate, and oxide-scale characteristics are not fully established.
The hypothesis is falsified if HEAs show no significantly greater interfacial enrichment of slower-diffusing elements or no faster or more uniform protective-scale formation than the binary controls.
